q: Stanley Miller carried out his famous experiment on the origin of organic molecules while working as a student of:
x: Miller was a graduate student of Harold Urey at the University of Chicago, which is why it is called the Miller–Urey experiment. Oparin and Haldane proposed the hypothesis that the experiment tested.

q: The two scientists who proposed the chemical-evolution hypothesis in the 1920s were Oparin and Haldane. Their nationalities were, respectively:
x: A.I. Oparin was a Russian (Soviet) biochemist and J.B.S. Haldane was a British scientist; they reached similar ideas independently.

q: The idea that living things arise from non-living matter is called:
x: Abiogenesis means life from non-life. Biogenesis is the principle that life comes only from pre-existing life.

q: The term 'chemical evolution' refers to:
o: The change in the chemistry of species after life began
The formation of organic molecules from simple inorganic substances before life existed
The breakdown of organic molecules by living cells
The evolution of new enzymes in modern bacteria
x: Chemical evolution is the slow build-up of organic molecules, and then polymers, from simple inorganic gases on the early Earth, before the first cells appeared.

q: Pasteur's swan-necked flask experiment showed that:
o: Microorganisms arise spontaneously from boiled broth
Air contains a vital force needed to make life
Organic molecules can form from inorganic gases
Microorganisms arise only from pre-existing microorganisms
x: Boiled broth in a swan-necked flask stayed free of microbes because dust and microbes were trapped in the bent neck. This supported biogenesis and disproved spontaneous generation under present conditions.

q: The gases of the Earth's primitive atmosphere are thought to have come mainly from:
o: Volcanic eruptions releasing gases from the Earth's interior
x: Early atmospheric gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia and hydrogen were released by volcanic outgassing. Photosynthesis came much later and added oxygen.

q: The oceans of the early Earth formed when:
o: Ice from comets melted after life began
Photosynthetic cells released water as a product
Underground rivers broke through the crust
The Earth cooled and water vapour condensed and fell as rain
x: As the young Earth cooled, water vapour in the atmosphere condensed and fell as rain for long periods, filling low areas to form the first oceans.

q: Later experiments of the Miller type, using similar gas mixtures and energy sources, also produced:
o: Functional enzymes such as DNA polymerase
Sugars and the nitrogenous bases of nucleotides
x: Later workers obtained sugars, nucleotide bases such as adenine, and other monomers. No experiment has produced a living cell or a complex functional enzyme.

q: Miller identified the organic products formed in his apparatus by using:
x: Miller analysed the solution with paper chromatography and detected several amino acids. Culturing would detect living organisms, which the sterile apparatus did not contain.

q: Sidney Fox heated dry mixtures of amino acids and obtained protein-like chains. These were called:
x: Fox called the heat-formed amino acid polymers proteinoids. When placed in water they formed small spheres called microspheres. Coacervates were Oparin's droplets.

q: When Fox placed proteinoids in water, they formed tiny cell-like spheres known as:
x: Proteinoids in water gather into microspheres, which have a boundary and can swell, shrink and bud. Coacervates are the related droplets described by Oparin.

q: RNA molecules that can act as catalysts are called:
x: Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules. Their discovery supports the idea that early life used RNA both to store information and to speed up reactions. Ribosomes are organelles, not single molecules.

q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they spontaneously form:
o: Small vesicles bounded by a lipid bilayer
x: Phospholipids arrange themselves into bilayer vesicles in water. This shows how a membrane-like boundary could have formed around early protocells without enzymes.

q: According to the heterotroph hypothesis, the first organisms obtained their energy by:
o: Fermenting organic molecules taken from their surroundings
x: The first cells were heterotrophs living in an organic-rich sea without free oxygen, so they broke down organic molecules anaerobically, as in fermentation.

q: The idea that the first living organisms took ready-made organic food from their surroundings is called the:
x: The heterotroph hypothesis says the first cells fed on the organic molecules of the primitive soup. Autotrophs that make their own food evolved later.

q: As the first heterotrophs multiplied, the organic molecules in the early seas were gradually used up. Which organisms would then have had the greatest advantage?
o: Cells that could only absorb ready-made amino acids
Cells that needed free oxygen to respire
Cells that had lost their ability to divide
Cells that could make their own food from simple inorganic substances
x: Once the soup ran low, cells that could make organic food themselves, such as early photosynthetic prokaryotes, could survive and spread. Oxygen was not yet available for aerobic cells.

q: Before the first cells existed, molecules had to form without help from living things. Which of these was therefore NOT available to drive chemical evolution?
o: A source of energy such as lightning or ultraviolet light
Simple gases such as methane and ammonia
Enzymes supplied by existing living cells
Water in which molecules could collect
x: Chemical evolution happened before life, so no enzymes from living cells were available. It needed raw gases, energy and water.

q: After the ozone layer formed, which major step in the history of life became possible?
o: Living things could move from water onto land
Organic molecules began to form from gases
Lightning first began to strike the Earth
x: Ozone screens out much harmful ultraviolet light. Before it formed, life was safest under water; afterwards organisms could survive on land.

q: Stromatolites, some of the oldest fossil evidence of life, are layered rock structures formed by:
o: Roots of the first land plants
x: Stromatolites form when mats of cyanobacteria trap and bind layers of sediment. Fossil stromatolites over 3 billion years old show that photosynthetic prokaryotes existed very early.

q: According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria were originally:
o: Aerobic bacteria taken into a larger host cell
x: The endosymbiotic theory says mitochondria came from aerobic bacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria, that lived inside a larger cell and became permanent partners. This helps explain the origin of eukaryotic cells.

q: Which observation supports the idea that mitochondria evolved from bacteria living inside early cells?
o: Mitochondria are found only in plant cells
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes
Mitochondria are made by the Golgi apparatus
x: Like bacteria, mitochondria have circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and divide by a fission-like process. Chlorophyll is found in chloroplasts, not mitochondria.

q: The Earth is about 4.6 billion years old and the oldest fossil cells are about 3.5 billion years old. Roughly how long after the Earth formed did cells appear?
x: 4.6 − 3.5 = 1.1 billion years. The figure 3.5 billion years is the age of the fossils, not the gap before life began.

q: Free oxygen first started to build up in the atmosphere only after:
o: Photosynthetic prokaryotes had been releasing it for a long time
x: Photosynthetic prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria released oxygen. At first it reacted with iron and other substances, so free oxygen built up only gradually. Ozone, eukaryotes and animals followed later.

q: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, who proposed the inheritance of acquired characters, was a:
x: Lamarck was a French naturalist. Weismann was German, Lyell an English geologist and Mendel an Austrian monk.

q: The scientist who cut the tails of mice to test inheritance of acquired characters, August Weismann, was a:
x: August Weismann was a German biologist. He is known for the germplasm theory and for his experiments on mice.

q: The germplasm theory was put forward by:
x: Weismann proposed the germplasm theory, which says only the germ cells carry hereditary material to the next generation. It opposed Lamarck's idea.

q: Lamarck explained the webbed feet of ducks and other water birds as the result of:
o: Birds with webbed feet surviving better and breeding more
A sudden mutation in a single duck
Ancestors stretching their toes while swimming and passing on the change
Separate creation of each kind of bird
x: Lamarck said water birds spread their toes as they swam, so the skin between them stretched, and this acquired change was inherited. Survival of birds already having webs is Darwin's explanation.

q: According to Lamarck, wading birds such as herons have long legs because:
o: Their ancestors stretched their legs to keep their bodies dry in water
Herons with long legs caught more fish and left more offspring
Long legs were caused by a single mutation
The legs grew because of disuse
x: Lamarck said the birds kept stretching their legs to avoid wetting their bodies, and the extra length was handed on. Selecting birds that already had longer legs is Darwinian.

q: Lamarck would explain the very small, poorly developed eyes of moles, which live underground, as the result of:
o: Use of the eyes in dim light
Disuse of the eyes over many generations
x: In Lamarck's view, moles living in darkness no longer used their eyes, so the eyes shrank and this reduction was inherited.

q: Lamarck believed that living things have an inner tendency to:
o: Become more complex and better suited over time
Stay the same as when they were first created
Produce far more offspring than can survive
Lose all organs that are used often
x: Lamarck thought organisms had an inbuilt drive towards greater complexity, together with use and disuse and inheritance of acquired characters. Overproduction was Darwin's postulate.

q: According to Lamarck, a completely new organ appears in an animal because:
o: A chance variation is preserved by natural selection
A gene is copied wrongly during meiosis
The organ is created suddenly in one generation
The animal feels a new need caused by a change in its surroundings
x: Lamarck held that a new need produced by a changed environment leads to new habits and so to new or altered organs. Chance variation and selection belong to Darwin's theory.

q: Lamarck's first law is the law of use and disuse. His second law states that:
o: The fittest individuals survive and reproduce
Changes gained by an individual during life are passed to its offspring
x: Lamarck's second law is the inheritance of acquired characters: changes produced by use or disuse are handed to the next generation.

q: A trait that is fixed by genes at fertilisation, and NOT gained during life, is:
o: The ABO blood group of a person
A scar left by a deep cut
Strong leg muscles of a regular runner
A tanned skin from working in sunlight
x: The ABO blood group is fixed by the alleles inherited from the parents. Scars, trained muscles and a suntan develop during life and are acquired.

q: Dog breeders have docked (cut short) the tails of certain breeds for many generations, yet the puppies are still born with full tails. This supports the view of:
o: Weismann, that changes in body cells are not inherited
Lamarck, that acquired changes are inherited
Darwin, that the fittest leave more offspring
Oparin, that life arose from chemicals
x: Cutting a tail changes only body (somatic) cells, not the germ cells, so the change is not passed on. This is just what Weismann's germplasm theory predicts.

q: Weismann used the term germplasm for:
o: The hereditary material in germ cells that passes from generation to generation
The cytoplasm of the body cells
The material that makes up the skin and muscles
The food stored in an egg
x: Weismann said the germplasm, carried in the germ cells, is continuous from one generation to the next and gives rise to both the gametes and the body. Changes in the body cells (somatoplasm) die with the individual.

q: Why can a mutation that occurs in a person's skin cell NOT be passed on to his children?
o: Skin cells are body cells and do not form gametes
Mutations are always repaired before birth
Skin cells contain only half the chromosomes
x: Only changes in germ cells reach the offspring. A skin cell is a somatic cell, so its mutation stays in that person's body.

q: Which change that arises during an organism's life CAN be passed on to its offspring?
o: A mutation in a cell that will form gametes
A scar formed after an injury
A larger brain from years of study
x: Changes in cells of the germ line can be inherited because they are carried in the gametes. Effects of exercise, injury or training are in body cells only.

q: Supporters of Lamarck argued that Weismann's mouse-tail experiment was not a fair test of Lamarck's theory. Their reason was that:
o: Weismann used too many generations of mice
Cutting off a tail is an injury, not a change caused by use or disuse in response to need
Mice do not normally have tails
Weismann cut the tails only of female mice
x: Lamarck spoke of changes produced by an animal's own use or disuse of organs. A tail cut by a scientist is an accidental injury, so critics said it did not test that idea; still, the experiment did show body changes are not inherited.

q: A fair-skinned family moves to a very sunny region and their skin becomes darker. According to Lamarck, children born to them afterwards would:
o: Be born with the original fair skin
Have darker skin only if a mutation occurred
Be born with darker skin than their parents had at birth
x: Lamarck believed acquired changes such as a tan are inherited. In reality a tan is a change in body cells, so the children are born with the family's inherited skin colour.

q: Which explanation of the great speed of the cheetah is Lamarckian?
o: Faster cheetahs caught more prey, survived and passed on their speed
Speed arose because slow cheetahs were eaten by lions
Speed came from a mutation that spread by chance
Ancestors ran hard to catch prey, their leg muscles grew stronger and this was inherited
x: Lamarck's explanation relies on effort during life (use) followed by inheritance of the gain. Survival of individuals that were already faster is the Darwinian explanation.

q: A student says, 'The bacteria became resistant because they needed to survive the antibiotic, and they passed this resistance on.' This explanation follows the idea of:
x: Saying that a need produces a change which is then inherited is Lamarckian. In fact a few bacteria were already resistant and were selected, which is Darwin's natural selection.

q: Which statement gives a Lamarckian, NOT a Darwinian, explanation?
o: Snakes lost their legs because they stopped using them while crawling
Moths matching the bark colour were eaten less and left more offspring
Insects already resistant to a pesticide survived and multiplied
Finches with beaks suited to local seeds left more young
x: Loss of an organ through disuse, followed by inheritance of the loss, is Lamarck's idea. The other three describe selection acting on variation that already existed.

q: In Lamarck's theory, the variations that lead to evolution are:
o: Random and present before any need arises
Produced in response to the needs of the organism
Caused only by errors in copying DNA
Produced only in the germ cells
x: Lamarck thought variations arise purposefully, as a response to need and use. Darwin and modern genetics say variation is random and already present; selection then acts on it.

q: Before Lamarck, most naturalists in Europe believed that species were:
o: Fixed and unchanging since they were created
x: The common view was the fixity of species, each kind created separately. Lamarck was among the first to argue clearly that species change.

q: Lamarck published his theory in 1809 and Darwin's On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859. How many years separate the two?
x: 1859 − 1809 = 50 years. Lamarck's theory therefore came half a century before Darwin's.

q: An important gap shared by the theories of both Lamarck and Darwin was that neither could explain:
o: Why organisms are suited to their surroundings
Why fossils are found in rocks
How characters are actually passed from parents to offspring
x: Both lived before genetics was understood, so neither knew how traits are inherited. Mendel's work and later genetics filled this gap.

q: Darwin sailed on HMS Beagle in the role of the ship's:
x: Darwin joined the Beagle as an unpaid naturalist. He collected plants, animals, fossils and rocks wherever the ship stopped.

q: Darwin's voyage on HMS Beagle lasted about:
x: The voyage lasted from 1831 to 1836, about five years, much of it surveying the coasts of South America.

q: Darwin observed that individuals of the same species are not exactly alike. This basic observation is called:
x: Differences among individuals of a species are variations. Natural selection works on these differences.

q: The process by which individuals with favourable variations survive and reproduce more than others was named by Darwin:
x: Darwin called it natural selection. Artificial selection is done by humans, and use and disuse is Lamarck's idea.

q: In 1858, the theory of natural selection was first presented publicly in a joint paper by Darwin and Wallace to the:
x: Papers by Darwin and Wallace were read together at the Linnean Society of London in 1858, a year before On the Origin of Species was published.

q: Darwin summed up evolution as the gradual change of species from their ancestors and called it:
x: Darwin used the phrase 'descent with modification': species descend from common ancestors and change gradually through natural selection.

q: Darwin chose the term 'natural selection' because he saw that:
o: Nature creates new organs when they are needed
Every individual in nature breeds equally
Nature, like a breeder, decides which individuals survive and breed
Nature selects which acquired characters are inherited
x: Darwin compared nature with a breeder choosing animals to breed. In nature, the environment 'chooses' by letting better-suited individuals leave more offspring.

q: Competition between a lion and a hyena for the same prey is an example of:
x: The lion and hyena belong to different species, so their competition is interspecific. Intraspecific struggle is between members of the same species.

q: Two male deer of the same species fighting for a female is an example of:
x: Both deer belong to one species, so this is intraspecific struggle. Such contests decide which males pass on their genes.

q: Darwin explained the large, brightly coloured tail of the male peacock by:
o: Use and disuse of the tail feathers
Protection of the male from predators
Sexual selection, as females prefer to mate with males having showy tails
Inheritance of feathers damaged during fights
x: Darwin proposed sexual selection: traits that make males more attractive to females increase mating success, even if they do not help survival.

q: Cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli have all been produced from a single wild mustard species. This is an example of:
x: Farmers chose and bred plants with enlarged leaves, flower buds or stems over many generations, producing these vegetables. This is artificial selection.

q: Darwin noticed that the animals of the Galápagos Islands most closely resembled those of:
x: Galápagos species were similar to, but different from, those of nearby South America. Darwin concluded they descended from mainland colonists and changed after reaching the islands.

q: The variety of Galápagos finches, each with a beak suited to a different food, all arising from one ancestral species, is an example of:
x: Adaptive radiation is the evolution of many species from one ancestor, each suited to a different way of life. The finches are the classic example.

q: Why did finches on different Galápagos islands become different species?
o: Their populations were isolated on separate islands and each was selected for the local foods
All the finches changed their beaks by using them in different ways
The birds on all islands interbred freely and mixed their traits
A single mutation produced all the species at the same time
x: Isolation stopped interbreeding between island populations, and natural selection on each island favoured beaks suited to the available food. Over time the populations became separate species.

q: The rise in frequency of dark-coloured peppered moths in industrial areas of England is called:
x: Industrial melanism is the increase of dark (melanic) forms in areas darkened by industrial soot, caused by bird predation favouring the dark moths.

q: Natural selection acts directly on an organism's:
o: Phenotype, the traits that are expressed
x: The environment 'sees' the expressed traits (phenotype), such as colour or speed. Recessive alleles hidden in heterozygotes are not exposed to selection.

q: Darwin believed that new species form:
o: Only by the inheritance of acquired characters
Slowly and gradually, over very many generations
x: Darwin's view, influenced by Lyell, was gradualism: small favourable variations accumulate over long periods to produce new species.

q: In sexually reproducing organisms, new combinations of existing alleles on which natural selection can act are produced mainly by:
o: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis
x: Meiosis shuffles alleles through crossing over and independent assortment, and fertilisation combines them further. Mitosis copies cells without new combinations.

q: In a snowy region, a rabbit population has some white and some brown individuals. Foxes spot the brown rabbits more easily. Over many generations:
o: Brown rabbits will turn white by trying to hide
The number of brown rabbits will increase
White rabbits are expected to become more common
Fur colour will stay at the same ratio
x: White rabbits are camouflaged against snow, so more survive and breed, passing on the white colour. Individuals cannot change their inherited colour by effort.

q: In a herd of gazelles, the fastest runners escape cheetahs more often. Over many generations, what is expected?
o: Every gazelle becomes faster by training
The average running speed of the herd increases
The herd stops varying in speed
x: Faster gazelles survive and breed more, so alleles for speed become more common and the average speed rises. Training effects are not inherited.

q: Beetle P lives 2 years and leaves 10 offspring that survive to breed. Beetle Q lives 4 years and leaves 6 such offspring. In Darwinian terms:
o: Beetle Q is fitter because it lives longer
Beetle P is fitter because it leaves more fertile offspring
Both are equally fit because both reproduce
Neither is fit because both eventually die
x: Darwinian fitness is measured by the number of surviving, fertile offspring left, not by lifespan or strength. P leaves 10 against Q's 6.

q: A common misunderstanding of Darwin's theory is the claim that natural selection:
o: Acts on variations that already exist
Works only on variations that are inherited
Produces the variations that an organism needs
Leads to populations better suited to their environment
x: Natural selection does not create variation; variation arises from mutation and recombination. Selection only favours some existing variants over others.
